title: carousel throttle sweep scratch
content:
Context:
This is a personal scratchpad for a small experiment investigating a recurring oscillation pattern we see when enabling short 'burst windows' on the autoscaler + prefix cache behavior. I call the pattern a 'carousel throttle' (rapid handoff between hot and cold lanes causing throughput/latency wobble).

Goal:
- Reproduce the carousel behaviour deterministically and measure the amplitude (p50/p95/p99 delta) across configurations.
- Find quick mitigations that don't require major runtime changes: batch timeout tuning, cooldown hold, or simple token-prime.

Hypothesis:
- Oscillation is caused by interplay between autoscaler step-up (adds a new worker cold) and per-request KV-cache miss penalty when traffic cycles. Small windows of high qps -> new replicas -> cold caches -> latency spike -> autoscaler backs off -> hot nodes receive traffic again -> repeat.

Test matrix (quick):
- model: gpt-small-q4_0 (quantized)
- payload: 64 tokens avg, deterministic prompt
- hardware: a2-small-sim (2xA100-sim in env)
- client: vegeta 12.8 (scripted arrival patterns)
- load profiles: (A) steady 120 qps, (B) 4s burst to 600 qps every 30s, (C) staircase: 60->240 step every 20s, (D) burst-window w/ priming requests before each burst

Commands used (approx):
- vegeta attack -duration=5m -rate=600 -targets=... | tee out.bin; vegeta report -type=json out.bin > out-600.json
- curl -X POST https://dev.redwood/api/infer -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEV" --data @payload.json
- small script to prime prefix cache: ./prime.sh --n=8 --sleep=0.25

Key metrics captured:
- p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) per 10s bucket
- qps observed
- KV cache miss rate (from trace headers)
- replicas active (autoscaler logs)

Quick results (condensed):
Profile A (steady 120 qps):
- stable: p50=28ms, p95=65ms, p99=120ms
- cache miss rate ~7%

Profile B (4s bursts to 600 qps every 30s, no priming):
- immediate oscillation: bursts cause p95 -> 300-900ms, p99 spikes to 1.4s during 4s window
- after burst, autoscaler adds 1-2 replicas (scale up happens ~9-12s after burst start)
- when new replicas come up, cache miss jumps to ~65% for next 20s
- amplitude (p95 during burst vs steady) ~ +420ms

Profile C (staircase):
- stepping causes sawtooth: each up-step introduces a 15-25% increased p95 for ~12s then recovers
- total effective throughput less than expected because of throttling/fallbacks

Profile D (burst-window + prime 8 requests 1s before burst):
- priming reduces p99 spike magnitude by ~40-60% depending on timing
- p95 still increases but peak shorter (4-6s vs 8-12s)

ASCII viz (simplified, p95 across time buckets)
Time ->  |----30s----|----30s----|----30s----|
Profile B p95 (ms):  60  72  310  85  66  920  92  58  74  480 ...
Sparkline (rough):  ▁▁▂▄▁▁▇▁▁▂▆

Observations / quick notes:
- Autoscaler latency is a big contributor: scale decisions lag the bursts, leading to more cold replicas in the reaction window. If scale-up was preemptive or quicker, amplitude would reduce.
- KV cache miss amplification: when a replica boots, its cache is empty; a small number of misses early cause longer tail due to cold KV access plus increased queuing.
- Priming helps but is brittle: need accurate timing before bursts and increases total token cost. Better to change cooldown/hold policy.
- Batch timeout: bumping continuous-batch timeout from 20ms -> 40ms absorbed some small jitter (reduced p50 variance) but did not fix p99 spikes.
- Simple ramping the admission (soft-start) into bursts with short ramp of 50ms between requests drastically reduced the p99 but requires client cooperation.

Potential quick mitigations to try next:
1) Autoscaler: introduce a 2s "pre-warm" window where we create 1 replica when seeing repeated small spikes (policy tweak).
2) Replica warmup: run a lightweight background priming thread that replays common prefixes on new replicas until cache hit rate > X%.
3) Admission shaping: add soft-start to edge proxy to smooth ingress during known bursts.
4) Prefill on scale-up: run n priming reqs as part of replica init (cheap, maybe 4-8 requests).

Open questions / TODOs:
- How does model size affect amplitude? test with medium (gpt-med-q4_0) next — likely larger cost per miss.
- Quantization impact: rerun with q8/q4 differences; do misses become more expensive (I/O/CPU)?
- Can we detect carousel pattern in telemetry (replica churn + KV miss spikes) and auto-enable priming? Add rule to alerting.
- Run a cost analysis: priming adds token cost; is it cheaper than lost SLA credits/latency penalties?

Notes for pairing w/ eng leads:
- Evan: check quick autoscale policy change feasibility (pre-warm on 3 bursts within 60s).
- Maya: prototype replica init priming script and measure added startup time.

Raw attachments / data pointers:
- vegeta traces in s3: s3://redwood-bench/carousel/2025-10-03/{profile}.json
- autoscaler logs: gcloud logs filter "scale" proj=redwood-dev:logName=projects/...

Conclusions (scratch):
- Carousel throttle is reproducible with the burst-window pattern.
- Best low-effort mitigation today: priming on scale-up + short admission ramp at edge.
- Longer-term: autoscaler heuristics + replica warmup baked-in are better.

Short TODO list:
- [ ] Run same sweep with gpt-med (2025-10-07)
- [ ] Implement init priming prototype (Maya) (2025-10-10)
- [ ] Talk to SRE about transient autoscaler policy change (Evan) (2025-10-12)
- [ ] Cost calc: priming vs SLA credits (me)

Free-form scribbles:
- maybe call the metric 'carousel amplitude' = p95_peak / p95_baseline
- measure 'priming ROI' = token-cost-priming / (reduction in p99-duration * sla_penalty_rate)

End of scratchpad.
